results.finalAssistantText:
On and HOKA took the growth in performance running, not Nike’s franchise. Nike’s fiscal 2024 revenue was $51.4 billion [E24] versus $51.2 billion [E24] the prior year. HOKA wholesale was $1,126.1 million [E15], equal to 2.19% [C11] of that Nike total. All of Deckers was 8.34% [C13] of Nike’s fiscal 2024 revenue. On’s revenue rose 46.6% [E8] to CHF 1,792.1 million [E8]. Those are fast gains off a small base, not a transfer of Nike’s $51.4 billion [E24].

Nike’s own damage is a stall, not a collapse. Fourth-quarter revenue was $12.6 billion [E24], down 2% [E24]. NIKE Direct was down 8% [E24]. Wholesale was up 5% [E24]. Gross margin recovered to 44.7% [E24]. Fiscal 2023 free cash flow was $4,872 million [E11].

At the July 5, 2024 close of $75.43 [E16], Nike is 20.2 times [C28] reconstructed fiscal 2024 earnings and 23.4 times [C29] fiscal 2023 diluted EPS of $3.23 [E7]. The fiscal 2023 free-cash-flow yield is 4.23% [C32]. Deckers trades at 32.2 times [C30] fiscal 2024 earnings. That is a lower multiple than the share-gainer, not a distressed price. A five-year low could not be verified because daily prices did not load, and fiscal 2025 guidance was not in the readable portion of the June 27 release. Another flat year while On and HOKA keep compounding would make the stall look structural. A sustained wholesale rebound, with the margin recovery turning into growth, would make the multiple a reset. Neither is established.

This is research, not investment advice.

Only $TLN has banked a Big Tech check tied to a nuclear site, and it was for a campus, not for electricity. In the filings available through this cutoff, the reactor developers have no hyperscaler power contract.

$TLN sold the Cumulus campus next to Susquehanna to Amazon Web Services for gross proceeds of $650 million [E26]. Of that amount, $300 million [E26] was escrowed pending development milestones. Those milestones were met, and the escrowed $300 million [E13] was paid on 23 August 2024 [E13], allowing the campus to be developed to 960 MW [E13] of power consumption. The power contract is separate and still ahead: supply of up to 960 MW [E27], fixed-price commitments that increase in 120 MW [E27] increments, and an option under certain conditions to cap commitments at 480 MW [E27]. The 5 September 2024 deck describes those prices as fixed over 10-year [E34] terms, then repriced at market. Susquehanna’s owned capacity was 2,228 MW [E34] in the portfolio summary as of 30 June 2024 [E34]. Talen said it was still looking forward to executing power sales under the PPA [E13]. On 2 August 2024 [E33], Talen disclosed a FERC letter on the interconnection-agreement amendment that would let Susquehanna sell power to the co-located data center. The campus cash does not depend on that amendment. The electricity sales do.

$CEG announced on 20 September 2024 [E8] a 20-year [E8] power purchase agreement with Microsoft, which it called its largest ever [E9]. Microsoft will buy energy from a restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1, approximately 835 MW [E9], to match power its PJM data centers use with carbon-free energy [E9]. The unit is expected online in 2028 [E44]. Restart still needs NRC approval, and a separate license-renewal request would extend operations to at least 2054 [E44]. The filing states neither the contract price nor Constellation’s restart budget. This is a signed offtake on a shut plant, not cash received. The operating company reported second-quarter 2024 revenue of 4,406 million USD [E36] and net income of 814 million USD [E36].

$VST’s Microsoft and Amazon agreements are long-term renewable power purchase agreements, not nuclear offtake [E25]. $SMR reported revenue of $1.0 million [E23] for the quarter ended 30 June 2024 [E23], and described data-center conversations rather than a named hyperscaler order [E23]. $OKLO’s income statement for the quarter ended 30 June 2024 [E47] shows no revenue, with operating income of -17.8 million USD [E47]. Its cash came from the business combination, not from Big Tech [E24].

The company already paid by a hyperscaler is $TLN, for a campus beside an operating plant. The company with a named, long-dated hyperscaler offtake on a specific reactor is $CEG, with power still years and a license away. Unlicensed reactor designs remain a different bet from either contract.

Through 23 September 2024, the only listed nuclear operator that has cashed a Big Tech check is $TLN. In March 2024 it sold the Cumulus data-center campus next to Susquehanna to Amazon Web Services for gross proceeds of $650 million [E21]. The last $300 million [E10], held in escrow, was paid on 23 August 2024 after development milestones. That money is for land, power infrastructure and a powered shell, not twenty years of electricity. The power deal is separate: a fixed-price contract for up to 960 MW [E7], stepping up over ten-year terms. On 20 September 2024 it announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1, approximately 835 MW [E6], targeted for 2028 [E11]. The unit was retired in 2019 [E3]. No Microsoft payment, restart cost or contract price is in the 8-K, and the restart still needs an NRC review. Constellation is already a large utility — Q2 2024 revenue was $4,406 million [E31] — so this contract is future and incremental, not cash today.

Management describes data-center conversations, but the named paid work is a Romanian engineering study, not a US hyperscaler offtake [E27]. Vistra’s Microsoft and Amazon deals in the same search were renewable contracts, not nuclear [E3].

A bet that nuclear is getting Big Tech checks is, on the filings, a bet on $TLN’s campus sale plus a power ramp that is only partly authorized. A bet on $CEG is a bet that a shut reactor clears the NRC and comes back in 2028 [E11] at an undisclosed price. Neither filing shows that new reactors are being paid to solve the grid.

This is research, not investment advice.
